import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Dean's conjecture on cycles of length divisible by `k`

*References:*
- [arxiv/2605.02731](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.02731)
  **Existence of cycles of length divisible by 3 or 4**
  by *Ilkyoo Choi, Hojin Chu, Ringi Kim, Boram Park*, where this is Conjecture 1.1.
- [De88] Dean, N., Open problem, in Cycles and Rays. (1988).
- [DeLeSa93] Dean, N. and Lesniak, L. and Saito, A., Cycles of length 0 modulo 4 in graphs.
  Discrete Math. (1993), 133--139.
- [ChSa94] Chen, G. and Saito, A., Graphs with a cycle of length divisible by three.
  J. Combin. Theory Ser. B (1994), 277--292.
-/

open SimpleGraph

namespace Arxiv.«2605.02731»

/--
**Conjecture 1.1 (Dean, 1988).** For every integer $k \geq 3$, every finite simple graph with
minimum degree at least $k$ contains a cycle whose length is divisible by $k$.

A cycle has length at least `3`, so the divisor is never `0` and the statement is not
satisfied for a trivial reason. `SimpleGraph.minDegree` is `0` on a graph with no vertices and
on a graph with no edges, so the hypothesis excludes both.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 5]
theorem dean_conjecture :
    answer(sorry) ↔ ∀ (k : ℕ), 3 ≤ k → ∀ (V : Type) [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V]
      (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj], k ≤ G.minDegree →
        ∃ m ∈ G.cycleLengths, k ∣ m := by
  sorry

/--
The case $k = 5$. This is the only case of the conjecture that is still open.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 5]
theorem dean_conjecture.variants.five :
    answer(sorry) ↔ ∀ (V : Type) [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V)
      [DecidableRel G.Adj], 5 ≤ G.minDegree → ∃ m ∈ G.cycleLengths, 5 ∣ m := by
  sorry

/--
The case $k = 3$, proved by Chen and Saito [ChSa94].
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 5]
theorem dean_conjecture.variants.three {V : Type} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V]
    (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj] (hG : 3 ≤ G.minDegree) :
    ∃ m ∈ G.cycleLengths, 3 ∣ m := by
  sorry

/--
The case $k = 4$, proved by Dean, Lesniak and Saito [DeLeSa93].
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 5]
theorem dean_conjecture.variants.four {V : Type} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V]
    (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj] (hG : 4 ≤ G.minDegree) :
    ∃ m ∈ G.cycleLengths, 4 ∣ m := by
  sorry

/--
The cases $k \geq 6$, proved by Liu, Ma and Zhao (2026). With [ChSa94] and [DeLeSa93] this
leaves `dean_conjecture.variants.five` as the only open case.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 5]
theorem dean_conjecture.variants.six_le {V : Type} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] {k : ℕ}
    (hk : 6 ≤ k) (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj] (hG : k ≤ G.minDegree) :
    ∃ m ∈ G.cycleLengths, k ∣ m := by
  sorry

/-- A graph with no edges has minimum degree `0`, so the hypothesis of the conjecture rules it
out. This is a check that the hypothesis carries weight. -/
@[category test, AMS 5]
theorem minDegree_bot_eq_zero : (⊥ : SimpleGraph (Fin 5)).minDegree = 0 := by
  decide

/-- The complete graph on four vertices has minimum degree `3`, so it is one of the graphs the
case `k = 3` applies to. -/
@[category test, AMS 5]
theorem minDegree_top_fin_four : (⊤ : SimpleGraph (Fin 4)).minDegree = 3 := by
  decide

end Arxiv.«2605.02731»

findings.description: The [DeLeSa93] bibliography entry gives pages 133–139. The cited article, “Cycles of length 0 modulo 4 in graphs,” appeared on pages 37–49. This is a reference error only; the k = 4 statement is faithful.
findings.source_evidence: The bibliography of arXiv:2605.02731v1, entry DLS93, gives Discrete Math. 121(1–3):37–49, 1993. The publisher-deposited Crossref record for DOI 10.1016/0012-365X(93)90535-2 independently gives page "37-49".

findings.description: The docstring attributes the k ≥ 6 result to “Liu, Ma and Zhao (2026)”; the first author is Luo, not Liu. The theorem statement and its solved status are correct.
findings.source_evidence: arXiv:2605.02731v1 cites LMZ2026 as Y. Luo, J. Ma, and Z. Zhao, “Dean’s conjecture and cycles modulo k,” arXiv:2601.13552. The latter paper’s author list is Yufan Luo, Jie Ma, Ziyuan Zhao, and its introduction explicitly resolves the conjecture for all k ≥ 6. https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.13552
findings.suggested_fix: Replace “Liu, Ma and Zhao” with “Luo, Ma and Zhao,” preferably linking to arXiv:2601.13552.

findings.description: The [De88] reference is bibliographically inconsistent: it lists “Open problem, in Cycles and Rays (1988),” whereas that volume is dated 1990. It also does not match the Dean reference supplied by the cited arXiv paper. The conjecture itself is correctly stated from Conjecture 1.1.
findings.source_evidence: The Dean1988 bibliography entry in arXiv:2605.02731v1 is Nathaniel Dean, “Which graphs are pancyclic modulo k?”, Sixth International Conference on the Theory and Applications of Graphs, Kalamazoo, Michigan, 1988. Springer’s catalogue identifies Cycles and Rays, edited by Hahn, Sabidussi and Woodrow, as a 1990 volume: https://link.springer.com/book/10.1007/978-94-009-0517-7 .
findings.suggested_fix: Replace [De88] with the Dean reference given in arXiv:2605.02731. If a separate Cycles and Rays reference is intended, supply its verified location and correct publication year.

review.notes: No mathematical misformalizations found in the seven declarations. The open/solved tags match the cited sources. The k = 3 and k = 4 declarations intentionally state special cases of Conjecture 1.1, not the stronger theorems also quoted in the paper. In /workspace/review/scratch.lean, I proved that the conclusion is equivalent to an explicit simple cycle of length 0 modulo k, that cycle lengths are at least 3, and that a positive minimum-degree bound implies nonemptiness and the usual per-vertex degree bound. I tested empty and small complete/edgeless graphs, proved the hypothesis is satisfiable for every k using K_(k+1), and constructed cycles for k = 3,4,5,6. The scratch file compiles; its verification lemmas do not depend on sorryAx. The older journal full texts were inaccessible through the publisher, so their results were checked against the explicit statements in arXiv:2605.02731 and their bibliography against Crossref.
